One month before admission he unloaded his truck in Kansas City during a rainstorm and then developed night sweats and cough.  

On arrival he was afebrile but hypoxic (SpO₂ 85 % on room air, requiring 2–3 L/min O₂). Labs showed a normal white blood cell count and elevated liver enzymes (AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated mild hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X‑ray revealed a diffuse reticulonodular pattern with hilar lymphadenopathy. He received empiric IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, doxycycline, and metronidazole.

Three sputum AFB smears were negative; MTB NAAT on sputum was not detectable.

Histoplasma antigen assays (serum and urine) and Cryptococcus antigen were negative. Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated (13.03 U/mL). Pathology showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; AFB and GMS stains were negative.  

Coccidioides serology returned positive: complement fixation 1 : 8, IgM ELISA positive, IgG ELISA negative, and immunodiffusion showed a partial identity reaction. Based on these data, liposomal amphotericin B was started, and azole/echinocandin therapy was discontinued.

case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old HIV‑1‑infected male farmer presented with a five‑day history of right hypochondriac abdominal pain, decreased appetite, nausea, vomiting, and two days of yellowish discoloration of the sclera. He denied fever, diarrhoea, visual changes, odynophagia, or dysphagia.  

He had been diagnosed with pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia four weeks earlier and was on a new antiretroviral regimen (raltegravir/darunavir/ritonavir).  

Physical examination revealed icterus and tender hepatomegaly; the remainder was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 10.7 g/dL) with normal leukocyte count, total bilirubin 9.2 mg/dL (reference 0–1), AST 109 U/L (15–37), ALT 41 U/L (14–59), and alkaline phosphatase 906 U/L (46–116). Serologies for hepatitis B and C were negative.  

Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated hepatomegaly (liver span 18 cm) with grade I–II intra‑hepatic biliary dilatation, a focal parenchymal lesion, and a common bile duct measuring 14 mm suggestive of obstruction at the ampulla, though no definitive mass was seen.  

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) showed an edematous papilla with stenosis and a dilated common bile duct with a pre‑papillary stricture, findings interpreted as suggestive of AIDS cholangiopathy. A wide papillotomy was performed and a 7 Fr CBD stent placed for drainage. Bile aspirate was negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora, and Mycobacterium. Brush cytology of the stricture revealed inflammatory cells, pigment‑laden macrophages, and red blood cells, with no acid‑fast organisms. An ampullary biopsy was obtained (results pending).

1. AIDS‑related cholangiopathy is common in patients with low CD4 counts and presents with jaundice and biliary strictures; the ERCP findings of papillary edema and pre‑papillary CBD stricture are classic. | "ERCP ... revealed oedematous papilla with stenosis. Cholangiogram showed a dilated CBD with prepapillary CBD stricture. All these features were suggestive of AIDS cholangiopathy."
2. Opportunistic parasitic infections (Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora) can cause similar cholangiopathy, but were excluded by negative bile aspirate. | "Bile aspirate was negative for Cryptosporidium, Microsporidium, Cyclospora, and Mycobacterium."
3. Mycobacterial infection (including Mycobacterium avium complex) may produce biliary obstruction; brush cytology showed no acid‑fast organisms, further lowering its likelihood. | "Brush cytology of the stricture ... with no acid‑fast organisms."
4. Viral etiologies, especially cytomegalovirus, are known causes of AIDS cholangiopathy; histopathology of the ampullary biopsy demonstrated characteristic viral inclusions (nucleomegaly with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic inclusions), supporting CMV as the pathogen. | "Cells of submucosal Brunner's glands showed nucleomegaly with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic cytoplasmic ... inclusions."
5. The patient improved clinically after biliary drainage and did not receive specific anti‑CMV therapy, which aligns with the self‑limited nature of CMV‑related cholangiopathy once obstruction is relieved. | "After intervention, the patient had immediate symptomatic relief and did not receive any anti‑CMV treatment. Liver enzymes normalised 2 weeks later."

case_prompt:
A 65‑year‑old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation was admitted for fever, chest pain, and dyspnea. CT chest angiogram showed bilateral ground‑glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy without emboli. He was initially treated for community‑acquired pneumonia with ceftriaxone and doxycycline, but fevers persisted for three days. On hospital day 6, antimicrobial therapy was broadened to vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, and azithromycin because of worsening hypoxia; the regimen continued for 10 days. HIV testing returned positive with an RNA level >500,000 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 15. On day 9 he required intubation; bronchoalveolar lavage identified Pneumocystis jiroveci (PCR and microscopy) and cytomegalovirus (viral culture). He received sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim and glucocorticoids for 21 days and was extubated on day 23.

He became lethargic and was re‑intubated on day 27. Intermittent fevers continued for 25 days with altered mental status. Vancomycin and piperacillin‑tazobactam were restarted. Initial work‑up for encephalopathy showed normal ammonia (18 µmol/L), normal CT head with and without contrast, and negative blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool cultures. EEG demonstrated moderate encephalopathy without epileptiform activity. HAART (elvitegravir, cobicistat, emtricitabine, tenofovir alafenamide) was begun on day 33 after genotype testing. Dexmedetomidine and piperacillin‑tazobactam were stopped on days 32 and 37 for possible drug fever, without fever resolution.

MRI of the head on day 37 revealed acute infarcts in the bilateral thalami, right parietal lobe, and right basal ganglia; neurology attributed these to embolic phenomena from atrial fibrillation. The patient also developed persistent non‑bloody diarrhea; bacterial and parasitic stool studies were negative. Serum CMV PCR on day 43 was 2,623,108 IU/mL. New nuchal rigidity and right lower‑extremity weakness prompted a lumbar puncture on day 44 after another normal head CT. CSF analysis was reported as consistent with encephalitis.

1. Persistent fever and encephalopathy in advanced HIV prompted evaluation for opportunistic infections; initial cultures and imaging were negative, suggesting a non‑bacterial cause. | "normal CT head with and without contrast, and negative evaluation for infection including blood, urine, tracheal aspirate, and stool cultures."
2. Drug fever from dexmedetomidine or piperacillin‑tazobactam was considered, leading to drug discontinuation, but fevers persisted, lowering its likelihood. | "There was concern for drug fever from dexmedetomidine and piperacillin‑tazobactam and both drugs were discontinued… After no improvement in fevers…"
3. Embolic strokes from atrial fibrillation were entertained after MRI showed acute infarcts; neurology favored an embolic origin, but infarcts did not fully explain nuchal rigidity or progressive weakness. | "MRI… showed acute infarcts… Neurology felt it was embolic phenomena from atrial fibrillation."
4. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis was a differential for acute encephalopathy, but CSF findings (not yet PCR) and lack of classic temporal lobe involvement made it less likely. | (Implied by “CSF analysis was consistent with encephalitis” without HSV‑specific comment.)
5. Tuberculous meningitis was considered given chronic meningitic picture, yet CSF profile lacked lymphocytic predominance and acid‑fast stains were not reported; absence of constitutional TB signs reduced probability. | (Inferred from negative evaluation for infection and lack of TB‑specific data.)
6. CMV infection became a leading diagnosis after a markedly elevated serum CMV PCR (2,623,108 IU/mL) and neurologic signs (nuchal rigidity, focal weakness). | "Serum CMV PCR… showing 2,623,108 IU/mL."
7. Confirmation of CMV CNS disease was achieved when CSF PCR detected CMV DNA, solidifying the diagnosis. | "CSF PCR for CMV DNA was positive."

case_prompt:
A 41‑year‑old morbidly obese woman with B‑cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia (RAI stage 0, 13q deletion, mutated IGHV) on active surveillance presented initially to urgent care with four days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a low‑grade fever (100.8 °F). She received IV fluids, anti‑emetics and was discharged with a presumptive diagnosis of acute gastroenteritis. One week later her gastrointestinal symptoms partially improved but persisted.

Ten days after symptom onset she presented to the emergency department with two days of dry cough, dyspnea, myalgias, and high‑grade fevers (102 °F). She was hypoxic (SpO₂ 85% on 6 L/min nasal cannula) and required escalation to a non‑rebreather mask and subsequent elective intubation with lung‑protective mechanical ventilation. Empiric antibiotics (cefepime, linezolid, doxycycline) were started. A posteroanterior chest radiograph demonstrated bilateral diffuse opacities. He had returned ten days earlier from a one‑week trip to Greece and reported unprotected sexual contact with a man two months before and during travel.  

On admission he was febrile (38.5 °C) and exhibited pharyngitis, oral candidiasis, and a skin rash. Laboratory studies showed elevated C‑reactive protein (18 mg/L), mild anemia (hemoglobin 10.5 g/dL) with low reticulocytes (37 × 10⁹/L), lymphopenia (500 cells/µL), neutropenia (600 cells/µL), and thrombocytopenia (90 × 10⁹/L). HIV‑1 serology was positive, confirmed by immunoblot, with a viral load of 5.47 × 10⁶ copies/mL and CD4⁺ count of 90 cells/µL. Neuroleptic (cyamemazine, risperidone) and benzodiazepine therapy were started for psychosis and anxiety, and the patient was transferred to the infectious diseases service.  

Two weeks after symptom onset, repeat HIV viral load was 6.85 × 10⁶ copies/mL with CD4⁺ count of 30 cells/µL and global lymphopenia (including CD8⁺ and NK cells). The immunoblot displayed gp120 and gp41 reactivity with weak ambiguous p24/p31 bands, a pattern compatible with acute primary infection; the patient had never been screened for HIV before. A review of records showed a normal lymphocyte count a year earlier. His recent partner was concurrently diagnosed with HIV.  

Lumbar puncture, EEG, and brain MRI were unremarkable. Thoraco‑abdominal and pelvic CT demonstrated homogeneous hepatosplenomegaly and several interstitial pulmonary lesions (micronodules and reticulations). Sputum cultures and bronchoalveolar lavage were negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Serologies for hepatitis A, B, C, E, toxoplasmosis, and syphilis were negative; EBV and CMV viral loads were undetectable. Genotypic testing identified an HIV‑1 CRF19‑cpx strain.  

Combination antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir, emtricitabine, raltegravir) was initiated two weeks after diagnosis, and cotrimoxazole prophylaxis for Pneumocystis pneumonia was started. Despite cART and neuroleptic treatment, psychotic symptoms, fever, chills, and sweats persisted, and the patient developed bilateral muscle rigidity. He required intensive care, and a neuroleptic malignant syndrome was diagnosed; extrapyramidal signs resolved after discontinuation of neuroleptics, yet fever and night sweats continued.  

Laboratory reassessment revealed worsening pancytopenia (hemoglobin 7.0 g/dL, platelets 50 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 600 cells/µL), hyperferritinemia, elevated transaminases, and mildly increased triglycerides. The team hypothesized hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) triggered by acute primary HIV infection. Sternal bone‑marrow aspiration showed macrophage activation without overt hemophagocytosis; stains for Leishmania were negative, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex PCR was negative. An empiric course of intravenous immunoglobulin (1 g/kg for 2 days) was given without clinical improvement.

case_prompt:
The patient had a childhood history of recurrent otitis media and a documented pneumonia at age 6. Physical features were typical of autosomal dominant Hyper‑IgE syndrome, including retained primary teeth, a broad nasal bridge, and a history of onychomycosis without mucosal fungal disease. He denied asthma.  

For several years he reported a mild, productive, clear‑coloured sputum each morning but no dyspnoea, weight loss, or fever. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated normal dynamic and static volumes as well as normal diffusion capacity.  

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) performed in April 2017 grew Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin‑sensitive) and Achromobacter species; a PCR panel was positive for an opportunistic pneumonia pathogen and the patient was treated with sulfamethoxazole‑trimethoprim. Subsequent BAL specimens (February 2018) showed no growth of bacteria, fungi, or mycobacteria; microscopy and PCR for Aspergillus species were negative, as was serum galactomannan. Serum Aspergillus‑specific IgG antibody was undetectable (0.0 AU/mL).  

Immunologic studies revealed normal IgG and IgM, markedly elevated IgA (6.22 g/L) and reduced IgG2 (1.53 g/L). Total serum IgE was mildly increased at 158 IU/mL (reference < 115). The interferon‑γ release assay was negative.  

Imaging showed a right‑upper‑lobe cavitary lesion with a “fungal‑ball”‑like appearance on HRCT (March 2017) and high FDG uptake on PET/CT (May 2017). Follow‑up scans demonstrated progression of the cavity and new infiltrates despite 11 months of voriconazole therapy. A repeat BAL cultured Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which was treated with intravenous tazobactam and ciprofloxacin; repeat galactomannan remained negative.  

Bronchoscopic brush biopsies yielded normal respiratory epithelial cells, and a CT‑guided coarse needle biopsy demonstrated chronic inflammation without malignant cells or any fungal elements.

Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis considered because of cavity with “fungal‑ball” appearance and PET FDG uptake, but excluded by multiple negative Aspergillus cultures, PCR, galactomannan, serology, and biopsy lacking fungal elements. | "BAL was negative for Aspergillus sp. and other fungal moulds... PCR and microscopy for Aspergillus sp. were negative as well... CT‑guided biopsy showed chronic inflammation with no evidence of ... any fungal infection."

The BAL culture for Mycobacterium sp. was negative as well. The interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) test was also negative."

case_prompt: A 79‑year‑old man with a known history of triple‑negative primary myelofibrosis presented in August 2021 after a syncopal episode. On admission his performance status was ECOG 2. Physical examination revealed pallor, tachycardia (91 bpm), a newly appreciated cardiac murmur, multiple rapidly enlarging purple skin lesions on the head, and palpable hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies showed severe anemia (hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL) and a markedly elevated white‑blood‑cell count of 249.4 × 10⁹/L (reference 3.5–9.8 × 10⁹/L). Platelet count was mildly decreased at 127 × 10⁹/L. Lactate dehydrogenase was markedly increased (1101.6 U/L; reference 125–248 U/L). Differential count demonstrated a neutrophil left shift with 4 % myeloid blasts and a basophil count of 1.5 %. Hydroxycarbamide was initiated, resulting in a rapid decline of the leukocyte count. Bone‑marrow evaluation revealed hypoplastic erythropoiesis and 10 % myeloid blast cells, findings that the authors interpreted as consistent with the patient’s prior diagnosis of atypical chronic myeloid leukemia.

1. Extreme leukocytosis with circulating blasts suggested a myeloproliferative neoplasm rather than a simple leukemoid reaction; “massively elevated WBC count of 249.4 × 10⁹/L… 4 % myeloid blast cells” supports a clonal process.  
2. Prior diagnosis of atypical CML was considered because marrow morphology showed 10 % blasts and hypercellular myeloid proliferation; “Bone marrow evaluation … 10 % myeloid blast cells, consistent with the previous diagnosis of atypical CML.”  
3. Reactive causes (infection, inflammation) were excluded by the presence of basophilia and blasts, which are atypical for a benign leukemoid reaction; “basophile count of 1.5 %” is a characteristic finding in CML.  
4. The definitive exclusion of atypical CML and confirmation of classic CML hinged on the detection of the Philadelphia chromosome; although this result is reported after the breakpoint, the authors state, “balanced translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11)… BCR::ABL positivity was confirmed,” which ruled out other myeloproliferative disorders.  
5. The skin lesions were initially thought to represent leukemic infiltration but later proved to be a CD8⁺ T‑cell lymphoma; “Initially, CD117 positivity led to the assumption of CML skin involvement… later identified as CD8+ T‑cell lymphoma,” demonstrating that cutaneous findings were not the primary diagnostic clue for the leukemic process.  
6. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which developed later, was identified as an opportunistic infection secondary to immunosuppression, not the cause of the initial hematologic abnormalities; “developed pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia… confirmed by PCR” – this infection was a complication, not the primary diagnosis.

Acid‑fast bacilli were identified in concentrated sputum and gastric aspirate smears. A 78‑year‑old woman from a rural community presented with worsening dyspnea, mild fever, and polyarthralgia. A 23‑year‑old Malay factory worker presented with a one‑month history of generalized headache, nausea, and vomiting. Two weeks later he noted painless, progressive blurring of vision in the right eye, describing an inferior visual field defect. case_prompt:
A 43‑year‑old Hispanic man presented with a 2‑week history of frontal headache, fever, nausea, and vomiting. Past history was notable for herpes zoster ophthalmicus two years earlier. Vital signs on admission were within normal limits. Neurologic examination showed mild cervical stiffness and pain with neck motion; no focal deficits were observed.

Laboratory studies revealed a normal white blood cell count (6.7 k/µL), anemia (hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL), and a normal platelet count (172 K/µL). A rapid HIV test was reactive; CD4 count was 83 cells/µL and HIV viral load 51,080 copies/mL. Serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was reactive with a titer of 1:1024, and CSF VDRL was also reactive, leading to a diagnosis of neurosyphilis. Initial CSF analysis showed 73 leukocytes/mm³ (96 % lymphocytes), protein 112 mg/dL, and glucose 37 mg/dL. The patient was started on ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and acyclovir, then switched to intravenous penicillin for neurosyphilis.

Three days later his headache and neck pain worsened, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, and visual hallucinations. MRI demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the left middle cerebellar peduncle, vermis, and right cerebellar hemisphere. Repeat lumbar puncture showed 267 leukocytes/mm³ (74 % lymphocytes), protein 94 mg/dL, glucose 8 mg/dL, and a positive CSF cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:640. India ink stain and fungal culture were negative. He was treated with amphotericin B lipid complex and flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis, later transitioned to oral fluconazole.

After completing induction therapy and a two‑week course of intravenous penicillin, he was discharged stable. Two weeks later he began antiretroviral therapy (tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine and darunavir‑ritonavir). At one‑month follow‑up he reported malaise, dizziness, slurred speech, and left‑hand clumsiness. Examination revealed an ataxic gait and saccadic eye movements. Repeat MRI showed improvement of supratentorial leptomeningeal enhancement but progression of posterior‑fossa leptomeningeal enhancement and T2/FLAIR signal abnormality.

He was readmitted; opening pressure on lumbar puncture was elevated (26 cm H₂O). CSF analysis revealed 2 leukocytes, normal glucose and protein, rare encapsulated yeasts on India ink, and a decreased cryptococcal antigen titer of 1:80. He was restarted on amphotericin B and flucytosine for a possible relapse of cryptococcal meningitis.

1. Neurosyphilis considered initially because serum RPR and CSF VDRL were reactive with high titers. | "Serum RPR was reactive with a titer of 1 : 1024 dils. VDRL from CSF was also reactive."
2. Cryptococcal meningitis diagnosed after CSF cryptococcal antigen returned strongly positive (1 : 640) and the patient improved with antifungal therapy. | "Cryptococcus antigen from CSF was positive with a titer of 1 : 640 dils... He was started on amphotericin B lipid complex and flucytosine for cryptococcal meningitis."
3. Bacterial meningitis deemed less likely given lymphocytic predominance, low glucose, and lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, plus negative Gram stain and cultures. | "CSF analysis revealed high WBC count (73 leukocytes/mm3) with lymphocytic predominance (96%)."
4. Relapse of cryptococcal meningitis suspected on readmission because of persistent symptoms, elevated opening pressure, and presence of rare yeasts on India ink despite previous therapy. | "Opening pressure was elevated (26 cm H2O). India ink stain revealed rare encapsulated yeasts."

A 56‑year‑old German man who has sex with men (MSM) has been residing in Bangkok since late 2015. He began pre‑exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) two months after arrival and continued it until 21 November 2016, when worsening renal function (creatinine rising to 1.69 mg/dL, eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m²) prompted discontinuation.

case_prompt:
A 65‑year‑old Caucasian man presented initially with painless horizontal diplopia on left gaze. His past medical history included coronary artery stents, hypercholesterolaemia, and former heavy smoking. He denied intravenous drug use or sex with men. Medications were amlodipine, valsartan, clopidogrel, and rosuvastatin. Ophthalmic history was notable for left‑eye herpes simplex keratitis. Visual acuity was 6/9 right eye and 6/24 left eye; the right cornea was normal, the left showed stromal scarring without neovascularisation. Lenses, pupils, optic discs, and vitreoretinal examination were normal. He had left esotropia with left lateral rectus underactivity and right‑gaze‑evoked nystagmus. Colour vision testing was normal bilaterally, and automated visual fields were full. Laboratory studies (CBC, CRP, ESR, lipids, renal function) were unremarkable. Brain MRI demonstrated only minor bilateral pontine ischemic changes. He was not tested for syphilis and was diagnosed with a microvascular left sixth‑nerve palsy. The diplopia resolved spontaneously over three months, and the sixth‑nerve palsy persisted for six months before fully resolving.  

Six months later he returned with an eight‑week history of painless “smeared” vision in which yellow, red, and orange colours were seen vividly in both eyes. Visual acuities were 6/12 right and 6/30 left. Anterior segment examination was unchanged. Both pupils were dilated and did not constrict to light, accommodative targets, or 0.1 % topical pilocarpine. Optic discs now exhibited mild temporal pallor. Vitreoretinal examination remained normal and ocular motility was full. Automated visual‑field testing suggested a right superior defect, though reliability indices were low. Optical coherence tomography showed thinning of the retinal nerve‑fiber layer and ganglion‑cell layer in both eyes. Repeat brain MRI was unchanged.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Microvascular sixth‑nerve palsy considered for the first episode because of the patient’s vascular risk factors and isolated diplopia; subsequently labeled as “microvascular left 6th nerve palsy.” | "He was diagnosed with microvascular left 6th nerve palsy."
2. Painless bilateral visual loss with tonic (non‑reactive) pupils raised suspicion for a neuro‑ophthalmic infectious process; the lack of pupillary constriction to light, accommodative targets, or pilocarpine is characteristic of neurosyphilis and helped differentiate it from typical ischemic optic neuropathy. | "Both pupils were dilated with no constriction in response to light, accommodative targets or 0.1% topical pilocarpine."
3. Progressive visual deterioration despite appropriate penicillin therapy prompted consideration of an autoimmune optic neuropathy; skin‑biopsy immunofluorescence showing nonspecific IgE, IgM, and C3 deposition and the emergence of auto‑antibodies supported this secondary diagnosis. | "We hypothesise his progressive visual loss was due to the development of autoimmune optic neuropathy, ... skin biopsy positive for immunoreactant deposition, ... development of autoantibodies (cardiolipin IgG, anti‑smooth muscle)."

A 67‑year‑old man was admitted for progressive elevation of liver enzymes. Over the next two months he developed distal weakness and numbness that spread proximally, ataxia requiring a walker, right‑sided weakness, and intermittent severe radiating back pain. Imaging of the head, brain, and spine was unremarkable. On admission he reported anorexia, 18‑lb weight loss, weakness, lower‑extremity edema, “rusty” colored urine, and sharp pains in his back, groin, and legs lasting minutes to hours. Ten days prior he noticed a non‑itchy painless rash that began on his arms and spread to his torso, palms, and thighs. He denied alcohol, tobacco, or drug use. He was sexually active with 5–10 male partners in the past year. No recent travel, sick contacts, antibiotics, or herbal supplements.

Physical examination showed mild scleral icterus, bilateral pitting edema of the lower extremities, and diminished pinprick and light‑touch sensation in both legs. The skin displayed a nontender maculopapular rash on the palms, thighs, chest, and scalp. A 1–2 cm nontender chancre was present on the posterior penile shaft.

Laboratory studies revealed total bilirubin 5.9 mg/dL, AST 201 U/L, ALT 116 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase 1,048 U/L. Abdominal CT demonstrated hepatomegaly with heterogeneous attenuation, patent hepatic vasculature, no focal lesions, and mild splenomegaly. HIDA scan showed patent cystic and common bile ducts. MRCP showed no extra‑hepatic biliary obstruction. A liver biopsy was performed.

A 93‑year‑old Caucasian woman was referred for a three‑month history of right cervical adenopathies. Past history included cutaneous sarcomatoid carcinoma of the face excised four years earlier. She denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, respiratory symptoms, or prior tuberculosis exposure. Physical examination revealed an enlarged, mobile, painful right cervical lymph node; the remainder of the exam was unremarkable.

Contrast‑enhanced CT of the cervico‑thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic region showed a right cervical mass with multiple adenopathies and fibrotic lesions in the upper right lung lobe; no other adenopathies or neoplastic lesions were identified.

Subsequent work‑up identified an IgG‑lambda monoclonal gammopathy; renal function, calcium metabolism, hemoglobin, urinary free light chains, and beta‑2‑microglobulin were all normal. Peripheral blood immunophenotyping demonstrated a polyclonal B‑cell population. Serologies for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were negative. An interferon‑γ release assay (QuantiFERON) returned positive.

Two months later the cervical adenopathies enlarged and developed cutaneous fistulization with suppurative lymphadenitis. Swab culture grew Staphylococcus aureus, treated with cefuroxime with only modest improvement. Excisional biopsy of the node showed granulomas with caseous necrosis and suppuration. PCR testing of the tissue was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Nocardia, Mycobacterium avium complex, Toxoplasma gondii, Aspergillus fumigatus, Bartonella spp., Treponema pallidum, and Leishmania infantum.

case_prompt:
A 9‑month‑old boy was admitted for a two‑week history of dry cough and wheezing, with tachypnea for five days. He was the second child of non‑consanguineous parents; birth history was unremarkable. He had three prior lower‑respiratory‑tract infections requiring hospitalization and one course of methylprednisolone before referral.

On exam his weight‑for‑age Z‑score was 0.60; respiratory rate 66 bpm, heart rate 156 bpm, temperature 36.6 °C. He had suprasternal and supraclavicular fossa depression, coarse breath sounds bilaterally without rales. Liver and spleen were non‑palpable.

Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (30.61 × 10⁹/L, 41.1% neutrophils), hemoglobin 130 g/L, hs‑CRP < 1 mg/L, ESR 8 mm/h, LDH 323 U/L (reference 135‑215). Immunoglobulins were markedly low: IgA 0.04 g/L (ref 0.10‑0.56), IgG 0.15 g/L (ref 3.60‑9.20); IgM 0.48 g/L was normal. T‑cell subsets (CD19⁺, CD20⁺, CD4⁺, CD8⁺) were within normal limits. Chest computed tomography revealed bilateral ground‑glass opacities. On hospital day 7, bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and lung biopsy were performed under general anesthesia. 6. Autoimmune interstitial lung disease considered; however, all autoimmune serologies were negative, making it less probable. | "Antinuclear, anti‑double‑stranded DNA, ... anti‑neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative."

He had a 3‑day history of non‑bilious, non‑bloody vomiting and a 2‑week history of increasing abdominal distension and scrotal swelling. The pregnancy was complicated by moderate oligohydramnios and decreased fetal movements, leading to urgent cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 1970 g (20th percentile); APGAR scores were 8 and 8 at 1 and 5 minutes. He required brief CPAP and nasal cannula oxygen for 3 days, had a normal post‑natal brain ultrasound, TSH 12 mU/L, and was discharged after 6 days. Immunizations were up‑to‑date, including PCV13.

On examination the infant was alert, irritable, pale and grunting. He was tachycardic (175 bpm) and tachypneic. The abdomen was markedly distended, tense and shiny with large ascites; no hepatosplenomegaly was palpable. There was substantial scrotal edema. Weight (with edema) was 3.5 kg (z score ‑3.83), length 52.5 cm (z score ‑4.31), head circumference 35.5 cm (z score ‑3.35).

- Malaria rapid diagnostic test positive for Plasmodium falciparum; thin blood smear identified P. falciparum‑infected red cells (1.846 × 10³ parasites/µL).

- Blood group A Rh‑D negative.

Plasmodium falciparum malaria is confirmed by a positive rapid diagnostic test and visualization of parasites on thin smear, providing definitive evidence for the diagnosis. | "Malaria rapid diagnostic test (MRDT) for P. falciparum was positive; thin blood smear showed P. falciparum malaria species with 1.846 × 10³ malaria‑infected red blood cells."

A 65‑year‑old immunocompetent man presented with an 11‑year history of a huge erythematous erosive plaque on his neck. Laboratory examinations were negative for syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus, peripheral blood lymphocyte abnormalities, microscopic examination for Mycobacterium leprae, IgM and IgG against NDO‑LID and MMP‑II (leprosy), acid‑fast staining of sputum smear, and anti‑Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibodies. The enzyme‑linked immunospot assay for tuberculosis (T‑SPOT.TB) and leprosy were also negative. Histopathology of the neck lesion demonstrated necrosis and epithelioid‑cell granuloma in the dermis, infiltrated by lymphocytes, epithelioid cells, and Langhans giant cells; periodic acid‑Schiff, silver, and Ziehl‑Neelsen stains were negative. Single polymerase chain reaction tests for rpoB and hsp65 genes of the skin lesions did not identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but nested PCR for the same genes was positive. Tissue cultures from the lesions grew caseous yellow colonies at 37 °C on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium after 40 days. Sequencing of the isolate’s 16S ribosomal RNA and hsp65 gene showed 100 % homology to Mycobacterium tuberculosis strain FDAARGOS_756.

Physical examination showed a 25‑kg weight loss in five months, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy on ultrasound, hypoesthesia to touch and painful stimuli, bilaterally thickened neural trunks, inability to fully flex the fingers, and dactylitis. Laboratory studies demonstrated microcytic, hypochromic anemia; serum protein electrophoresis was normal. Serologic testing for HIV, T‑Spot.TB, syphilis (VDRL), and hepatitis B and C were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis was normal. Chest computed tomography was unremarkable; abdominal CT confirmed hepatosplenomegaly.

Electroneuromyography showed an asymmetrical sensory and motor axonal neuropathy with focal slowing of conduction velocity and severe impairment of the ulnar nerves at the elbow and tibial nerves at the ankle. Peripheral‑nerve ultrasonography revealed hypertrophic neuropathy of the ulnar, median, left peroneal, and tibial nerves (most evident at pre‑tunnel levels) with intraneural hyperemia of the left ulnar nerve and mild thickening of the right peroneal nerve.

A 46‑year‑old woman presented with erythematous papules, papulopustules, and a plaque on the right lower limb that had been present for more than two years. She had previously been diagnosed with dermatitis and eczema at other hospitals and was treated with oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, ebastine) and topical glucocorticoids (mometasone furoate, halometasone) without improvement; the rash gradually enlarged. The patient’s past medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus for over 10 years, managed with metformin 0.5 g three times daily. Glycemic control had been satisfactory early on (fasting 6–7 mmol/L, postprandial 9–10 mmol/L) but later became poorly monitored; she recalled postprandial glucose values of 20–30 mmol/L around the time of tattooing and 13–15 mmol/L around lesion onset. She denied use of immunosuppressive agents or known immunodeficiency.

Physical examination showed only the cutaneous lesion on the right lower limb and red and blue‑black tattoos in the same area. HIV testing was negative. Routine blood work, T‑ and B‑cell subsets, renal and hepatic panels, treponemal serology, rapid plasma reagin, and immune indices (ANA, ENA, immunoglobulins, complement) were all within normal limits.

A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the lesion revealed fungal hyphae. Tissue cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 °C produced numerous dense grey‑black colonies. Microscopic examination of the colonies showed septate, hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia 2.5–3 µm in diameter, arising in chains from palisade‑like phialides directly attached to broadly clavate vesicles. Matrix‑assisted laser desorption/ionisation‑time of flight mass spectrometry identified the organism as *Aspergillus fumigatus*.

Skin biopsy demonstrated a reticulate cornified layer with oval spores within the corneous layer, a mildly thickened epidermis, and a sparse perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes and neutrophils in the superficial dermis. Periodic acid‑Schiff staining was positive, and spores were visualized within the stratum corneum.

Other cutaneous fungal infections (e.g., dermatophytes, Candida) were considered, but culture characteristics (dense grey‑black colonies, septate hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia, clavate vesicles) and MALDI‑TOF identified *A. fumigatus*, distinguishing it from dermatophytes or yeasts | "Numerous ... fungal colonies grew that were dense, and grey‑black... septate and hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia... identified as A. fumigatus."

A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for the preceding month, with a noticeable increase in pallor one week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Systemic examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and a small palpable lymph node in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed bi‑cytopenia: platelet count 11 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 97 mg/L, white‑blood‑cell count 10.2 × 10⁹/L, and reticulocyte count 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑blood‑cell fragmentation (schistocytes) at 1.45 % and neutrophilic toxic granulation. LDH was 1,021 U/L, AST 46 IU/L, ALP 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L (direct 12.7 µmol/L). Urinalysis revealed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was 1.72 g/L. Coombs test was negative.

Initial management assumed atypical immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); the patient received two doses of IVIG 1 g/kg without response, and platelet and hemoglobin levels continued to fall. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed; the aspirate showed megakaryocytes suggesting immune destruction, while the biopsy revealed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas. Viral serologies for EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative, and QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest/abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy.

Given the patient’s recent consumption of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese in a Brucella‑endemic region, Brucella serology was obtained and returned with titers of Brucella abortus 1:5,120 and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480 (both markedly elevated). A regimen of doxycycline (5 mg/kg orally twice daily) and rifampin (20 mg/kg orally twice daily) was started for six weeks. Following initiation of anti‑brucellosis therapy, the patient no longer required fresh frozen plasma transfusions, and his platelet and hemoglobin levels began to improve, with a concurrent decline in LDH.

A 78‑year‑old man residing in a Tibetan rural temple was admitted for recurrent low back pain of 5 years’ duration that had markedly worsened over the preceding 3 months. He had type 2 diabetes (diagnosed 2003) and a history of L1‑2 vertebral tuberculosis treated surgically in 2015 with debridement, bone grafting, internal fixation, and a 12‑month course of HRE (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol) chemotherapy. In September 2016 he underwent percutaneous endoscopic lumbar decompression for spinal stenosis.

Since July 2018 he noted persistent lumbago and a progressively enlarging right‑sided lumbar mass extending from T10 to L2, which grew from roughly 10 × 20 cm to 20 × 35 cm. He denied cough, sputum, or fever. Routine labs on 11 Oct 2018 showed elevated procalcitonin, C‑reactive protein, ESR, leukocytosis, and anemia. CT of chest and lumbar spine demonstrated partial L1‑2 bone defects, intervertebral space stenosis, and a lobulated low‑density lesion in the right paravertebral psoas muscle. He was started on isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and levofloxacin, but the mass continued to enlarge.

On admission (18 Oct 2018) physical examination revealed tenderness from T9 to L3 and a palpable 20 × 35 cm mass on the right lumbar region. Hemoglobin was 110 g/L, fasting glucose 8.44 mmol/L, and liver/kidney functions were normal. Eight sputum smears for bacteria, fungi, and mycobacteria were negative. Enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed multiple low‑density masses within the right erector spinae, psoas major, and quadratus lumborum muscles (largest ≈12.2 × 10.1 cm) with mild ring enhancement. MRI of the thoracolumbar spine showed irregular nodular and patchy lesions from T10 to L3, hyperintense on T1 and T2, involving the right psoas major, quadratus lumborum, erector spinae, and subcutaneous tissue (largest ≈12.4 × 9.1 cm).

On 19 Oct 2018, percutaneous aspiration of the mass yielded ≈50 mL of purulent, turbid fluid. Microscopy showed numerous nucleated cells, moderate red blood cells, a few pus cells, and a few gram‑negative rod‑shaped bacteria.

A 19‑year‑old man from the Andean region of Peru, employed at a poultry market for the past 7 months, presented with a 3‑week history of dry cough, headache and a feverish sensation. Five months earlier he had a brief episode of cough with mild hemoptysis that resolved spontaneously. Physical examination revealed decreased vesicular murmur over the left anterior hemithorax with wet crackles. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, leukocyte count 11 277 /mm³ (eosinophils 162), CRP 244 mg/L, and D‑dimer 2.72 µg/mL. Serologies for HIV, HTLV, hepatitis B and C were negative. Bronchoscopy revealed inflammation and erythema of the left upper bronchus with active bleeding; bronchoalveolar lavage samples were obtained for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture. Empiric anti‑tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) and intramuscular codeine were started while awaiting results. case_prompt:
A 28‑year‑old man from a peri‑urban area of Lima, employed as a motorcycle taxi driver, presented to the emergency department after 34 days of persistent fever, chills, weight loss, dyspnea, and leukocytosis. Five years earlier he had completed individualized therapy for multidrug‑resistant pulmonary tuberculosis.  

Initially he experienced moderate left rib‑cage pain, palpitations, and high fever; an electrocardiogram was normal and a chest X‑ray performed on day 4 of illness was reported as “normal.” Fever (38 °C) and chills continued, alongside neutrophilic leukocytosis. He also developed abdominal pain and weight loss. Serology for HIV 1‑2 was non‑reactive and three sputum samples were negative for acid‑fast bacilli. Abdominal ultrasound and stool studies were unremarkable, leading to hospital admission for persistent symptoms.  

On examination the patient was thin, with a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg, oxygen saturation 96 % on room air, moderate dehydration, and abolition of vesicular breath sounds over the middle and lower thirds of the left hemithorax. Laboratory studies showed rising leukocyte counts and C‑reactive protein.  

On hospital day 9 (illness day 42) thoracentesis yielded 600 mL of purulent, greenish fluid; a thoracic drainage tube was placed. The following day intravenous antibiotics were started. By hospital day 12 (illness day 45) fever and leukocytosis resolved, and the drainage fluid was no longer purulent. A CT scan on day 15 (illness day 48) demonstrated a marked reduction in left‑sided pleural fluid volume. Subsequent chest ultrasound on day 22 (illness day 55) measured the residual empyema at 73 mL.  

Initial work‑up for tuberculosis included HIV and HTLV serology (both non‑reactive) and sputum and urine cultures for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, all negative. GeneXpert MTB/RIF performed on pleural fluid was also negative.

1. Tuberculous empyema considered because of prior multidrug‑resistant TB; excluded by multiple negative microbiologic tests – “Culture and smear tests for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum and urine were also negative” and “both of which were negative” for MGIT and GeneXpert.  
2. HIV‑associated opportunistic infection considered given immunosuppression; excluded by serology – “Serology for immunodeficiency virus infection (HIV 1‑2) … were nonreactive.”  
3. Non‑tuberculous bacterial empyema suspected; definitive pathogen identified by mass‑spectrometry – “The MALDI‑TOF MS test was used for detecting common germs and was positive for P. micra.” This finding, together with the dental source, confirmed an anaerobic oral flora‑related empyema.

She denied cough, fever, night sweats, skin rashes, neurological symptoms, recent trauma, malignancy, diabetes, hypertension, corticosteroid use, or other immunocompromising conditions. There was no known exposure to birds or soil.

On admission, vital signs were normal (temperature 37 °C, pulse 80 bpm, respirations 20/min, BP 124/87 mm Hg). Physical examination revealed increased skin temperature, swelling, tenderness over the right lateral ankle, a positive varus trigger test, palpable dorsalis pedis pulse, and intact peripheral circulation. MRI of the right ankle showed multiple patchy long T1 and long T2 signals beneath the articular surface, focal involvement of the distal fibula, extensive soft‑tissue and muscular swelling, enhancing lesions with abscess formation, blurred and narrowed joint space, and unevenly thickened, markedly enhancing synovium—findings consistent with an infectious process involving the ankle joint.

A 9‑year‑old boy with no prior medical problems was referred to the emergency department for a 10‑day history of fever and productive cough. He was born in India; his father had been diagnosed with tuberculosis a year earlier. He had completed a 7‑day course of amoxicillin‑clavulanic acid prescribed by his pediatrician, after which he was afebrile for only one day.

On arrival his temperature was 39.4 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, peripheral oxygen saturation 98‑99 % on room air, and respiratory rate was normal. Physical examination revealed right basal hypophonesis with diffuse wheezing. Laboratory studies showed an elevated C‑reactive protein of 39.5 mg/L (reference 0‑5 mg/L), a normal total white‑blood‑cell count of 7,890/mm³ with neutrophils 6,050/mm³ (reference 1.5‑6.0 ×10³/mm³). Hepatic and renal panels were within normal limits.

A chest radiograph demonstrated a right hilar, round‑shaped area of parenchymal hypoventilation surrounded by additional medio‑basal hypoventilation, described as compatible with a tubercular excavation. Given the suspicion of active pulmonary tuberculosis, the patient was admitted, isolated, and a QuantiFERON‑TB test was performed, together with microscopic, molecular, and culture studies on three sputum samples; all were negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

Bedside lung ultrasound identified three consolidated parenchymal areas with air‑arborized bronchograms and a left basal pleural effusion. Because of persistent radiologic concern, a chest CT scan was obtained, revealing bilateral areas of parenchymal consolidation with irregular, confluent margins and partially obstructed bronchi, ground‑glass opacities, numerous centrilobular micronodules some showing a tree‑in‑bud pattern, and several mediastinal lymphadenopathies, some containing internal necrosis.

High clinical suspicion for tuberculosis led to initiation of first‑line antitubercular therapy, which was stopped after six days due to intolerance. To obtain a definitive diagnosis, bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was performed; microbiologic analysis of the BAL fluid excluded Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, prompting discontinuation of antitubercular treatment.

Typical bacterial pneumonia (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae) considered due to productive cough and fever; less likely because white‑blood‑cell count was normal, CRP modestly elevated, and imaging showed extensive mediastinal lymphadenopathy and tree‑in‑bud pattern atypical for ordinary bacterial pneumonia. | "Physical examination revealed right basal hypophonesis, with diffuse wheezing... Chest CT scan... areas with ground‑glass appearance and several centrilobular micronodules, some of which had a tree-in‑bud aspect."

Viral pneumonia (including common respiratory viruses) considered given age and fever, but the presence of consolidations with air‑arborized bronchograms, necrotic lymph nodes, and lack of viral prodrome made this less plausible. | "Bedside lung ultrasound showed 3 consolidated areas of parenchyma with air‑arborized bronchograms and left basal pleural effusion."

case_prompt:
A 16‑year‑old boy presented to the outpatient department with lower back pain radiating to both lower limbs, associated with difficulty walking and prolonged sitting. The symptoms began six months earlier and were initially managed with analgesics, but worsened over the past two weeks. MRI of the lumbar spine showed destruction of the D12 and S1 vertebral bodies with a paravertebral collection. Laboratory studies demonstrated a white blood cell (WBC) count of 15,000/µL with 80% polymorphs, platelet count of 510,000/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 60 mm/h, and C‑reactive protein of 40 mg/L. Both the Mantoux test and Interferon‑γ Release Assay were negative.

A CT‑guided vertebral biopsy was performed; during the procedure the radiologist noted parenchymal lung lesions. Histopathology revealed dense acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrates without granulomas or malignancy. Acid‑fast bacilli smear was negative, and the sample was not sent for Gene Xpert MTB/Rif Ultra. Aerobic cultures grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptible to all tested pseudomonal antibiotics. The patient initially improved on targeted antibiotics, but two months later deteriorated, with WBC rising to 18,800/µL (88% polymorphs). Repeat CT demonstrated nodular lesions in the lungs, spleen, and liver.

Anti‑tubercular therapy (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) was started. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and endobronchial ultrasound‑guided transbronchial subcarinal lymph node biopsy were performed. BAL cytology was unremarkable, but Gene Xpert MTB/Rif Ultra on BAL was “positive (trace)” with “indeterminate” rifampicin resistance. Immunohistochemistry showed CD3 and CD20 positivity (reactive lymphocytes) and was negative for CD15 and CD30 (ruling out Hodgkin disease). Gene Xpert on lung and lymph node biopsies was negative, and mycobacterial cultures from BAL, lung, and lymph node specimens remained negative.

Because of the indeterminate rifampicin result and lack of clinical response, a regimen for presumed drug‑resistant tuberculosis (moxifloxacin, amikacin, clofazimine, linezolid, cycloserine, para‑aminosalicylic acid) was initiated, but after two weeks there was no improvement. A review of the radiographic studies raised suspicion for malignancy, prompting a CT‑guided biopsy of left para‑aortic lymph nodes.

1. Tuberculosis was considered due to vertebral destruction and pulmonary nodules; however, Mantoux and IGRA were negative, AFB smear was negative, repeat Gene Xpert on lung and lymph node specimens was negative, and mycobacterial cultures remained sterile. | "Both the Mantoux test and Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) were negative... Gene X‑pert MTB/Rif Ultra on lung biopsy and lymph node was negative, and Mycobacterium cultures from all specimens ... were also negative."
2. Drug‑resistant TB was entertained after an indeterminate rifampicin result, but lack of clinical improvement despite a second‑line anti‑TB regimen and persistent negative microbiology argued against it. | "In light of the indeterminate rifampicin result and lack of response to initial treatment, a diagnosis of drug‑resistant TB was made... case_prompt:
A 27‑year‑old man with trisomy 21 and intellectual disability presented with a 6‑month history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, inspiratory stridor, night sweats, and recent voice loss, dysphagia, and choking on all consistencies. He had previously consulted nine physicians across ENT, pulmonology, gastroenterology, and allergy services in both Mexico and the United States and had received multiple courses of antibiotics for presumed pneumonia, antihistamines, inhaled bronchodilators, and systemic glucocorticoids without significant improvement. He denied diabetes, known immunodeficiency, or travel aside from brief trips to Mexico, and he regularly consumed unpasteurized dairy products from Mexico. Social history revealed residence with his mother in El Centro, California, frequent visits to an aunt in Mexicali, and exposure to areas with high prevalence of homelessness and illness; his mother denied known tuberculosis contacts.

An outside‑hospital computed tomography scan reported findings compatible with epiglottitis and a right upper‑lobe cavitary lung lesion, prompting transfer. On arrival he displayed inspiratory stridor, dysphonia, and dyspnea. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed a boggy, edematous epiglottis with copious white frothy secretions and exophytic supraglottic masses that partially obstructed the airway. An awake tracheostomy was performed for airway stabilization, followed by direct laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy with biopsies. Intra‑operative inspection revealed diffuse firm, pseudo‑tumor‑like ulceroproliferative lesions involving the epiglottis, false vocal folds, ventricle, arytenoids, and true vocal folds. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a normal tracheobronchial tree without lesions.

Histopathologic examination of the laryngeal tissue showed granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis, epithelioid histiocytes, chronic inflammatory cells, and multinucleated giant cells.

2. Lack of response to antihistamines, inhalers, and systemic glucocorticoids argues against an allergic or purely inflammatory airway disorder. | "He … trialed … antihistamines, inhalers, and glucocorticoids without significant improvement."

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) was considered but deemed unlikely because of the patient’s epidemiologic exposure, presence of a cavitary lung lesion, normal admission CBC, and absence of sinonasal, renal, or cutaneous findings. | "Autoimmune causes such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) were considered; however, GPA was felt less likely given the patient's epidemiologic risk factors, cavitary lung lesion, normal admission CBC, and absence of sinonasal, renal, or cutaneous involvement."
4. Primary laryngeal malignancy could produce exophytic supraglottic masses, yet the biopsy demonstrated granulomatous, caseating inflammation rather than malignant cells. | (implicit from) "Histopathologic examination … showed granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis …"
5. Mycobacterial tuberculosis is supported by the combination of chronic constitutional symptoms, cavitary lung lesion, caseating granulomas on tissue histology, and high‑risk exposure (unpasteurized dairy, endemic region). | "A positive MTB‑RIF GeneXpert from the outside hospital and early biopsy histopathology showing caseating granulomas with a rare AFB further supported a mycobacterial etiology over autoimmune vasculitis."

case_prompt:
A 23‑year‑old female presented to the skin department with a large ulcer over the left side of the neck, as well as ulcers over the left axilla and chest wall that included a discharging sinus. She reported weight loss, loss of appetite, and intermittent fever. Two years earlier she had developed neck swellings for which she received Category II antituberculous therapy (ATT) for six months, without resolution; the swellings subsequently enlarged, and she was diagnosed with Rosai‑Dorfman syndrome and treated with systemic steroids for three months. 

On examination she looked ill, was malnourished, and anemic. There was matted cervical lymphadenopathy on the right side of the neck. An irregular ulcer 5 in × 3 in covering the left sternomastoid muscle had a slough‑covered floor; its base was indurated and formed by matted lymph nodes. Two additional irregular ulcers were present over the left axilla and chest wall, one with a discharging sinus, tethered to underlying indurated tissue. 

Clinically, multidrug‑resistant tuberculosis (TB), NTI, and immunodeficiency were considered as differentials. Hemogram showed anemia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate without leukocytosis. Touch smear and sputum were negative for tuberculous bacilli. Mantoux test was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. HIV I and II serology were negative. Pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Biochemical parameters were normal. Histology revealed a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the dermis. She was empirically restarted on ATT Category II together with cotrimoxazole, but showed very little clinical response. Consequently, cultures were repeated; there was no growth from the discharge on blood agar, MacConkey agar and thioglycollate broth after 48 h of incubation.

1. Multidrug‑resistant TB considered due to chronic ulceration and prior ATT, but excluded because “Touch smear and sputum were negative for tuberculous bacilli,” “Mantoux test was negative,” and “There was very little clinical response to the above treatment.”  
2. Immunodeficiency (especially HIV) considered given non‑healing ulcers, but excluded as the patient was “negative for HIV I and II.”  
3. Common bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus) considered because “Pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus,” yet excluded since “There was very little clinical response to the above treatment” with antibiotics and the ulcers persisted.  
4. Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (NTI) remained plausible; definitive support came when “culture was repeated, which this time grew non pigmented, smooth colonies on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium on 7th day of inoculation at 37 °C,” and “The isolate reduced nitrate, was urease positive and sensitive to amikacin,” leading to molecular identification as “M. chelonae‑abscessus.”  
5. Successful targeted therapy with clarithromycin (“Within 2 weeks of institution of clarithromycin, the axillary ulcer and sinus healed… At the end of 40 days… the ulcer over the neck completely healed”) further confirmed the diagnosis.

A 4‑year‑old boy from a rural area was brought to the Emergency Department with fever, severe persistent diffuse headache, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss. case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old man, working as a priest, presented with a 2‑year history of generalized raised nodular lesions. Two years ago he noticed small reddish lesions over the right knee that gradually enlarged and ruptured with blood‑stained purulent discharge. Similar lesions later appeared on the left knee, both elbows, and ears. The lesions were not associated with loss of sensation, pain, itching, burning, joint pain, swelling, or fever. He consulted a local doctor who performed a biopsy that was reported as suggestive of fungal infection; consequently he received itraconazole and amoxicillin‑clavulanic acid without improvement. No acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) staining was performed at that time.

On examination, multiple erythematous nodules and plaques ranging from 3 mm to 3 cm were present on the bilateral ear pinna and over bony prominences of the extremities (elbows, knees, malleoli, dorsal feet). Some lesions had hemorrhagic crusts. The nodules were nontender, firm to hard, without oozing, sinus formation, or ulceration. There was no known contact with leprosy patients.

Baseline blood tests were normal. Slit‑skin smears and biopsies from several lesions were obtained for bacterial and fungal cultures because subcutaneous mycoses were initially suspected. Microscopy and culture for both bacteria and fungi yielded negative results.

Standard nerve conduction studies demonstrated mild axonal sensory mononeuritis multiplex in the bilateral upper limbs and axonal sensory polyneuropathy in the bilateral lower limbs, with thickening of the greater auricular, ulnar, and common peroneal nerves.

Tuberculoid or other cutaneous mycobacterial infections considered; less likely because lesions were painless, chronic, and lacked ulceration, and initial biopsy suggested fungal rather than mycobacterial pathology. | "biopsy report was suggestive of fungal infection; hence, the patient was treated with itraconazole… without any relief."
3. Peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex and polyneuropathy) pointed toward an infectious neuropathic process such as leprosy rather than pure fungal disease. | "Standard nerve stimulation test was done which showed evidence of mild axonal sensory mononeuritis multiplex… with bilateral greater auricular, ulnar, common peroneal nerves showing thickening."
4. Detection of numerous acid‑fast bacilli on modified Ziehl‑Neelsen stain confirmed Mycobacterium leprae infection, establishing leprosy. | "Examination of stained smear revealed characteristic AFB in large numbers… A bacterial index of 4+ (10 AFB per oil immersion field) was recorded."
5. Histopathology showing diffuse polymorphous infiltrate with foamy histiocytes and AFB highlighted by Fite‑Faraco stain corroborated leprosy and excluded fungal organisms. | "AFB were highlighted by Fite‑Faraco stain…"

case_prompt:
A 52-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, and prior rituximab presented with a one‑week history of fevers, chills, headache, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, nonproductive cough, fatigue, and a month of night sweats. He worked as a truck driver, traveling throughout the Midwest, and had unloaded his truck in Kansas City during a rainstorm one month before admission. On arrival he was afebrile but hypoxic (SpO₂ 85% on room air, requiring 2–3 L/min oxygen). Laboratory studies showed a normal white blood cell count and elevated liver enzymes (AST 74 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 170 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly; chest X‑ray showed diffuse reticulonodular densities with hilar lymphadenopathy. He received empiric IV ceftriaxone, azithromycin, doxycycline, and metronidazole. Initial infectious work‑up was negative for respiratory viruses, Histoplasma urine antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Legionella urine antigen, HIV, acute hepatitis, HSV PCR, CMV PCR, QuantiFERON‑TB, and sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii DFA. Rheumatology held methotrexate and sulfasalazine.

Chest CT demonstrated diffuse micronodularity in all lobes with perilymphatic and centrilobular distribution, scattered calcified granulomas, mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly—findings suggestive of a miliary pattern. Three sputum AFB smears were negative; MTB NAAT on sputum was not detectable. Bronchoscopy showed endobronchial nodules and plaques; BAL Aspergillus galactomannan and PJP DFA were negative. Serum Aspergillus galactomannan, Histoplasma antigens, and Cryptococcus antigens were all negative, but Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated (13.03 U/mL). Biopsy revealed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation; AFB and GMS stains were negative. Coccidioides serology returned positive (CF 1:8, IgM positive, IgG negative) with a partial identity reaction on immunodiffusion. Given concern for an invasive fungal infection, empiric anidulafungin plus posaconazole was started, later switched to liposomal amphotericin B while discontinuing the azole and echinocandin.

1. Tuberculosis considered due to miliary imaging pattern and night sweats, but excluded by multiple negative tests – “Three sputum AFB cultures were collected and were smear negative… NAAT was not detectable… T‑SPOT interferon‑gamma release assay was negative.”  
2. Invasive aspergillosis considered because of diffuse micronodules, but excluded by negative antigen and culture data – “Aspergillus galactomannan antigen… negative” and “Aspergillus fumigatus IgG was elevated… but cultures remained negative.”  
3. Coccidioidomycosis raised as a leading diagnosis based on serology – “Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation assay returned positive at 1 : 8, Coccidioides IgM by ELISA was positive, and Coccidioides IgG by ELISA was negative… This pattern of serological data suggested active coccidioidomycosis.”  
4. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia considered given immunosuppression, but excluded – “sputum Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) negative” and “BAL PJP DFA… negative.”  
5. Common bacterial community‑acquired pneumonia evaluated; excluded by lack of response and negative antigen tests – “Respiratory viral PCR, Histoplasma urine antigen, Streptococcus pneumoniae urine antigen, Legionella urine antigen… all negative.”  
6. Other endemic fungi (Histoplasma) initially low suspicion because antigen tests were negative – “Assays for serum Histoplasma antigen enzyme immunoassay (EIA)… were negative.” However, eventual culture and DNA probe confirmed the diagnosis – “The isolate was preliminarily identified as Histoplasma capsulatum… DNA probe… positive.”

case_prompt:
A 34‑year‑old man presented with high‑grade fever with chills and rigors and left‑sided pleuritic chest pain associated with a lump in the anterior chest wall. He had stage 5 chronic kidney disease and was on regular hemodialysis via an arteriovenous fistula, awaiting kidney transplantation.

Pyogenic (bacterial) septic arthritis was considered but deemed unlikely because the swelling was non‑tenderly fluctuant, skin temperature was normal, there was no discharging sinus, and subsequent cultures were negative for pyogenic organisms. | "There was no superadded pyogenic infection being ruled out by final pus culture and sensitivity report."

case_prompt:
A 5‑year‑old boy from rural Sabah presented with a one‑month history of headache, right eye pain, vomiting, difficulty walking, blurred vision, and fluctuating consciousness, accompanied by weight loss and anorexia. He had received BCG vaccination but missed other immunizations. On exam his GCS was 9 (E2V2M5), he had left lateral strabismus, unequal sluggish pupils (4 mm/3 mm), and symmetric 4/5 strength in all limbs with normal reflexes; Babinski was downgoing and Kernig’s sign was absent.

Non‑contrast CT showed acute hydrocephalus with cerebral edema, and an external ventricular drain was placed, revealing high opening pressure and clear CSF. MRI demonstrated diffuse enhancing nodular leptomeningeal thickening, especially at the basal cisterns, without intra‑axial lesions; small non‑enhancing cystic lesions were noted along the leptomeningeal surface.

A tuberculous meningitis work‑up was performed. ESR was 90 mm/h and CSF protein was elevated with normal glucose. Mantoux test was negative; blood, CSF, and CSF cultures were negative for organisms. After 14 days his condition improved, and ophthalmology showed right visual acuity 1/60 and no light perception in the left eye with a positive afferent pupillary defect. He was discharged after a 4‑week stay.

One month later he returned with vomiting, unsteady gait, and anorexia. Repeat MRI showed markedly more extensive nodular leptomeningeal enhancement and enlargement of the previously seen cystic lesions. MR spectroscopy of the thickened tentorium cerebelli revealed a markedly elevated choline:creatine ratio of 4.34 and absence of a singlet peak at 3.8 ppm. A transcranial biopsy was performed during revision of his external ventricular shunt, and dural tissue was obtained for analysis.

2. Overt TB infection was deemed unlikely due to multiple negative microbiologic tests. | "The Mantoux test was negative, and the blood, CSF, and CSF TB cultures showed no organism... The CSF for acid‑fast bacilli as well as CSF GeneXpert were also negative."

case_prompt:
A 62‑year‑old woman was admitted with nine days of paroxysmal falls and impaired consciousness and four days of paroxysmal limb twitching with gibberish speech. Initial tonic‑clonic seizures progressed to frequent tonic seizures with right‑ward head turning, resembling faciobrachial dystonic seizures, occurring >10 times per day. Prior brain MRI was normal. Initial antiseizure therapy (sodium valproate, diazepam, levetiracetam) yielded no improvement. She denied hypertension, coronary disease, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, mental illness, hepatitis, tuberculosis, and had no family history of hereditary disease.

On admission: temperature 36.3 °C, heart rate 91 /min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 162/85 mmHg. Neurologic exam showed cognitive dysfunction (poor memory, poor calculation) with otherwise normal cranial nerves, motor strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait, and no meningeal signs.

Routine blood tests, coagulation, liver and kidney panels, glucose, lipids, serology for hepatitis B, syphilis, HIV, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, thyroid antibodies, and tumor markers were all normal except low serum chloride (95 mmol/L). Serum auto‑immune encephalitis panel was notable only for anti‑LGI1 antibody titer 1:16 (normal < 1:10); all other neuronal antibodies (NMDAR, CASPR2, GABABR, DPPX, GAD65) and paraneoplastic antibodies were negative.

CSF analysis showed slight lymphocytic leukocytosis (10 × 10⁶/L) with normal opening pressure, appearance, glucose, chloride, Gram stain, acid‑fast stain, ink stain, metagenomic NGS, and CSF neuronal antibodies. CSF treponemal testing was positive (TPPA) and non‑treponemal testing (RPR) was positive.

Serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was positive at 1:16 and TPPA positive. CSF TPPA and RPR were also positive.

EEG demonstrated irregular medium‑ to high‑amplitude slow waves with occasional sharp waves in the right temporal lobe, spreading bilaterally. Brain MRI revealed increased T2/FLAIR signal in the medial right temporal lobe with mild‑moderate gadolinium enhancement; magnetic resonance angiography was normal. Chest CT, echocardiography, abdominal and urinary ultrasounds, electromyography, and nerve conduction studies were unremarkable.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neurosyphilis supported by serologic evidence: positive serum RPR (1:16) and TPPA, and concordant positive CSF TPPA and RPR, indicating intrathecal treponemal infection. | "The patient had a positive RPR with a serum titer of 1:16 and a positive TPPA. Subsequently, TPPA and RPR in CSF were tested, and both results were positive."
2. Anti‑LGI1 encephalitis considered due to serum anti‑LGI1 antibody (1:16) and limbic‑type seizures, but CSF LGI1 antibodies were absent and CSF pleocytosis was mild, making isolated autoimmune encephalitis less certain. | "serum ... anti‑LGI1 antibody with a titer of 1:16... The CSF showed slight leukocytosis ... AE‑related antibodies ... were normal."
3. Viral encephalitis (e.g., HSV, VZV) excluded by negative CSF metagenomic NGS, negative Gram/acid‑fast/ink stains, and lack of fever or classic imaging pattern. | "metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS), ... Gram staining, acid‑fast staining, ink staining ... were normal."
4. HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder ruled out by negative HIV serology. | "serological testing for ... HIV were negative."
5. Tuberculous meningitis excluded by negative acid‑fast stain, absence of typical CSF findings, and normal chest imaging. | "acid‑fast staining ... were normal" and "CT of the chest ... were normal."
6. Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis excluded by negative tumor markers and absent onconeural antibodies (anti‑Hu, anti‑Ri, anti‑Yo, etc.). | "serum tumor markers ... were normal" and "PNS‑related antibodies ... were normal."
7. Cerebrovascular etiology (vasculitis) considered but MRA showed no vascular stenosis or vasculitis‑like changes. | "MRA ... revealed no abnormalities."
8. Primary anti‑LGI1 encephalitis alone deemed possible but overlapping with neurosyphilis because both can produce limbic MRI changes and seizures; the presence of intrathecal treponemal antibodies tipped the balance toward neurosyphilis as the primary driver. | "Uncertainty arose as to whether the patient had both anti‑LGI1 encephalitis and NS or whether the LGI1 antibody and LE manifestations were due to the NS."

case_prompt: A 65‑year‑old man with a remote history of left radical nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) in 2002 and a recent diagnosis of stage II diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) treated with three cycles of R‑CHOP and consolidative radiotherapy presented in 2020 with non‑neutropenic fevers and rigors of unclear source. After a second dose of combination immune‑checkpoint inhibition (ipilimumab 1 mg/kg plus nivolumab 3 mg/kg), he returned to the emergency department with persistent fevers, acute kidney injury, and transaminitis. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics and isavuconazole were administered because of known pulmonary nodules. Imaging revealed new generalized lymphadenopathy in the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and diffusely avid splenomegaly on PET/CT. Differential diagnoses included recurrence of DLBCL, hyperprogression of metastatic ccRCC, immune‑related toxicity with a sarcoid‑like reaction, or other infectious/inflammatory causes. A left axillary fine‑needle aspirate and core biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation; stains for mycobacteria (Ziehl‑Neelsen) and fungi (GMS) were negative, and no malignant cells were identified. An extensive infectious work‑up was negative, including T‑spot, AFB blood cultures, coccidioides serologies, Q fever serologies, Bartonella serologies, blood histoplasma antigen, and histoplasma antibody. Given his farm exposures and splenic granulomata, histoplasmosis was considered despite negative serologies, while a sarcoid‑like reaction was also entertained but steroids were withheld because pulmonary function tests were normal and there were no parenchymal lung findings.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrence of DLBCL was plausible given prior lymphoma and new FDG‑avid nodes, but biopsy showed no lymphoma cells and was negative for malignant involvement. | "Left axillary fine needle aspirate (FNA) and core biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with ... negative for involvement with RCC, lymphoma, or other malignancy."
2. Hyperprogression of metastatic ccRCC was a concern because of systemic lymphadenopathy, yet tissue pathology did not reveal RCC cells and stains were negative for carcinoma. | "biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation ... negative for involvement with RCC ... or other malignancy."

Immune‑related sarcoid‑like reaction was entertained due to checkpoint‑inhibitor therapy, but steroids were not started because pulmonary function was normal and there were no parenchymal lung lesions. | "While a sarcoid-like reaction secondary to ICIs was also considered, steroids were not initiated given normal pulmonary function tests (PFTs) and lack of parenchymal manifestations."
4. Tuberculosis was excluded by negative Ziehl‑Neelsen stain and negative T‑spot/AFB blood cultures. | "negative stains for mycobacteria (Ziehl‑Neelsen stain) ... an extensive infectious disease evaluation was negative including T‑spot, acid‑fast bacillus (AFB) blood culture ..."

case_prompt: A 16‑year‑old male student from Jieyang City, Guangdong Province was admitted on 11 November 2020 with a 6‑month history of intermittent dry cough without fever, chest pain, or known exposures to birds or soil. Chest CT performed on 19 October at a local hospital showed a lung shadow suspicious for tuberculosis, prompting referral. On admission, physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 7.20 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 51.9 % (3.73 × 10⁹/L), and C‑reactive protein 9 mg/L. Both T‑SPOT and purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test were positive (13 × 14 mm). Serial sputum acid‑fast stains on 13, 14, and 15 November were negative. A chest plain film and contrast‑enhanced CT on 13 November demonstrated cavitary lesions in the left lower lobe and right lung, interpreted as possible pyogenic inflammation, fungal infection, or secondary tuberculosis. Empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam 2.25 g intravenously twice daily was started. After 10 days, repeat CT showed little change. Immunoglobulin levels, T‑cell subsets, and HIV testing were normal. Bronchoscopy on 17 November displayed congested and edematous bronchial mucosa throughout both lungs; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytology showed respiratory epithelium and few neutrophils, without malignant cells. Tracheoscopic brushings were similarly non‑diagnostic. BALF GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative, as were tests for MTB‑DNA and rpoB; the (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan assay was <37.5 pg/mL. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were observed microscopically. A second bronchoscopy on 20 November confirmed bilateral bronchitis, and BALF was sent for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered due to positive T‑SPOT, positive PPD, and cavitary lesions on imaging; excluded because multiple sputum smears and GeneXpert were negative and there was no radiographic response after anti‑tuberculous‑suspicion treatment. | "T‑SPOT and pure protein derivative (PPD) skin test (13 × 14 mm) were positive... GeneXpert (-): MTB‑DNA: negative, rpoB: negative."
2. Bacterial pyogenic pneumonia suggested by cavitary lesions and initial empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam; excluded because after 10 days of appropriate antibiotics, chest CT showed little change and cultures remained negative. | "After 10 days of regular treatment, the chest CT scan showed little change compared with pre‑treatment."
3. Common fungal infection (e.g., Aspergillus) entertained given cavitary lesions; G test was negative and microscopy showed no hyphae, lowering this possibility. | "G test revealed <37.50 pg/ml. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were found."
4. Malignancy considered during bronchoscopy; cytology of BALF and brushings showed no cancer cells, effectively ruling it out. | "Microscopic examination of bronchial lavage fluid (BALF) ... no cancer cells."
5. Opportunistic infection by Cryptococcus neoformans ultimately identified: unbiased mNGS of BALF yielded a specific read of C. neoformans, which was subsequently confirmed by CrAg‑LFA (titer 1:80) and fungal culture, establishing pulmonary cryptococcosis as the definitive diagnosis. | "mNGS result came back and showed one specific read of C. neoformans... CrAg‑LFA (titer 1:80) and fungal culture ... revealed as positive, confirming the mNGS detection."
